That kind of uncertainty can reshape where retirees shop, what brands they buy, and which businesses feel the squeeze or gain loyalty. This article walks through three stocks from our seniors exposed screener that could be helped by these shifts, and why their stories deserve a closer look.

The stocks below are just a starting sample from this idea, and the full screen surfaced 11 more U.S. discount retailers and consumer staples businesses with equally compelling narratives that are not covered in this article. Church & Dwight (CHD)

Church & Dwight fits directly into this seniors and value theme, with Arm & Hammer and other everyday staples filling shopping baskets at supermarkets, mass merchants, and dollar channels when older consumers look to stretch fixed incomes.

Church & Dwight develops household and personal care essentials like Arm & Hammer, OxiClean, Waterpik and Trojan that often appear on everyday shopping lists for budget conscious and senior consumers. Most sales come from Consumer Domestic at about US$4.8b, with Consumer International generating roughly US$1.2b and the Specialty Products Division around US$300 million. The business has a market value near US$25.8b.

"The strong trajectory of e commerce and online sales, with Church & Dwight's online channel now accounting for roughly 25% of global consumer sales, continues to support a mix shift toward higher margin, data rich distribution that can lift revenue and earnings quality over time."

title: Colgate-Palmolive vs. Kraft Heinz: With the Market Turmoil, Which Stock Is a Better Buy?

Colgate-Palmolive vs. Kraft Heinz: With the Market Turmoil, Which Stock Is a Better Buy?
Jack Delaney, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 10:35 PM CST 5 min read

WMT
KHC

Trading disclosure

With the recent market turmoil, investors may start looking more closely at defensive stocks like Colgate-Palmolive (NYSE:CL) and Kraft Heinz (NYSE:KHC).

Colgate-Palmolive dominates personal care categories like toothpaste, while Kraft Heinz focuses on massive scale within the packaged food industry. This comparison breaks down their latest performance and valuation to help you decide which belongs in your portfolio.

The case for Colgate-Palmolive

Colgate-Palmolive operates a diverse business model focused on oral care, personal care, home care, and pet nutrition. The company sells its products in more than 200 countries, reaching a vast global audience of consumers, dentists, and veterinarians. In its latest annual report, the company noted that Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) and its affiliates accounted for approximately 11% of sales. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $20.4 billion, which represented growth of approximately 1.4% compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $2.1 billion for the period. This resulted in a net margin of nearly 10.5%, indicating a decrease from the approximately 14.4% net margin recorded during the previous fiscal year.

The case for Kraft Heinz

Kraft Heinz is a global food and beverage giant producing items for at-home, restaurant, and on-the-go occasions. As a major player among food stocks, the company operates in multiple countries and relies on a mix of independent brokers and direct sales. In its latest annual report, the company noted that Walmart represented approximately 21% of net sales in FY 2025. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $24.9 billion, a decrease of approximately 3.5% from the previous year. The company reported a net loss of nearly $5.8 billion for the fiscal period. This led to a net margin of roughly -23.4%, which was a significant shift from the positive net margin reported in the prior fiscal year.

Risk profile comparison

Colgate-Palmolive faces risks from its extensive international operations, where foreign currency fluctuations and geopolitical instability can impact financial results. The company competes in an intense global market against private labels and direct-to-consumer brands that challenge its pricing power. Additionally, the company must manage the ongoing financial uncertainty and potential costs related to talc-related litigation.

Kraft Heinz deals with intense competition in the food and beverage industry and the constant need to predict shifting consumer preferences. The company is managing substantial indebtedness and recently announced the divestiture of its North American coffee business, which competes with brands like J. M. Smucker (NYSE:SJM). It also faces potential risks from U.S. tax audit disputes and recent non-cash impairment charges on its intangible assets.

Walmart has delivered strong share price gains in recent years. This puts fresh attention on a simple question for investors who focus on fundamentals: does the current price around US$125 reflect what its earnings can support?

Over the past 5 years, Walmart has returned 171.3%. This puts a lot of embedded optimism into the stock and raises the bar for what its earnings need to justify.

Recent moves into automation, drone delivery and data driven retail media may support expectations for how efficiently Walmart can convert future revenue into profit and cash flow.

Your read on Walmart is one view; the desks covering it have another. See what analysts think Walmart's shares could be worth.

The issue now is whether Walmart's earnings, relative to the Fair Ratio benchmark, are sufficient to support where the stock trades today.

If you are weighing Walmart's recent automation and AI push against its earnings, it can help to compare that story with other retailers and tech driven operators screened for 52 AI infrastructure stocks.

Does Walmart Look Fairly Valued on Earnings?

The P/E ratio is a useful shorthand for Walmart because earnings remain the key yardstick most investors use for a mature retailer that is investing heavily in technology. On this metric, the stock trades around 45.1x earnings. That sits well above the Consumer Retailing group on roughly 17.8x and also ahead of the peer set near 24.9x, which indicates buyers are already paying a premium for Walmart's earnings stream compared with many retailers.

The Fair Ratio model, which adjusts the benchmark for factors like growth prospects, profitability profile, size and sector risks, puts Walmart's current P/E only slightly above the level it would expect. The premium multiple therefore appears broadly aligned with what that framework suggests rather than significantly stretched. Because Walmart is committing about US$6b to automation over several years, the current P/E already incorporates an expectation that those supply chain and efficiency investments will matter, so you need to decide whether that story feels fully reflected in the price before reacting to the recent strength. Yahoo Finance reported on November 5 that the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5% into correction territory. Chip stocks took the brunt of the damage, as the leading AI chipmaker fell 9% to pace Dow decliners and another chip designer plunged 17%, the outlet reported.

The slide erased the gains from a day earlier, when the Dow had jumped nearly 1,600 points after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Yahoo Finance wrote on November 4. Even so, the blue-chip index finished Thursday just 1.9% below its record closing high of 54,349 from early August.

The Dow's Safe-Haven Run Cracks

For most of the week, the Dow had looked like the sheltered corner of the market. Yahoo Finance reported on November 2 that the Dow edged up 0.4% while the Nasdaq dropped roughly 1% as investors rotated out of technology names and into consumer cyclical and financial services shares. On Thursday, that cushion gave way, as the focus turned to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI buildout, and for the data centers driving it in particular. Data center power and infrastructure stocks fell by double digits, and the Nasdaq 100 was recently more than 10% below its October closing high. The reversal was fast. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at an equity research firm, pointed out that the VIX volatility index posted its biggest one-day jump in more than two years. It took the Nasdaq just six minutes to erase its entire post-election rally.

A Jobs Report Steadies the Tape

Friday brought a partial rebound. Yahoo Finance reported on November 6 that the US added 165,000 jobs in October, and the Nasdaq gained 1.9% while the S&P 500 rose 1% and the Dow added 0.1%. One could say the Walton family does not deserve to be rich. Among the world's wealthiest people, they are the only ones who did not start or serve as senior management of a company, most of which are in the tech industry. Nevertheless, five of Walmart (NYSE: WMT) founder Sam Walton's children and grandchildren have watched their combined net worth rise by $100 billion so far in 2026, Bloomberg reports. That is about the amount Oracle (NASDAQ: ORCL) founder Larry Ellison has lost in the same period.

Sam Walton started Walmart in 1942, at the age of 44. According to the Fortune 500, it was America's largest company for several years, until it yielded that position to Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) last year.

Niloo138 / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

Walmart remains a juggernaut. It employs 2.1 million people ("associates" as the company calls them). In the US, the figure is 1.6 million. Its footprint in its home market is 4,600 Walmart stores and 600 Sam's Club locations. Ninety percent of the US population lives within 10 miles of a Sam's Club or Walmart location.

In the most recent quarter, Walmart revenue rose 5.9% to $187.9 billion. Operating income rose 2.9% to $9.4 billion. John Furner, Walmart's President and CEO, said, "Our team delivered another good quarter, and we continue to make steady progress on the long-term value drivers of our business. Our multi-year growth in eCommerce is evidence that customers are choosing Walmart because we deliver price, speed, and convenience
across a broad assortment. At Walmart, they can have it all."

About Dollar Tree

Founded in 1986, Dollar Tree operates a nationwide chain of stores selling everyday household essentials, food, snacks, health and beauty products, seasonal merchandise, party supplies, and other general merchandise at value-oriented prices. For decades, the company primarily sold products at a base price of $1. However, that changed in 2021, when it announced and completed the rollout of a $1.25 base price point across its stores.

Valued at a market capitalization of $25.8 billion, DLTR stock is up 12% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. Should Dollar Tree stock find a place in your portfolio amid the changing political landscape? Let's take a closer look.

www.barchart.com
Bet Your Dollar on Dollar Tree, But Nothing More

Dollar Tree's strategy is primarily rooted in its specialized merchandising and operating model rather than proprietary technology. The retailer has developed longstanding direct relationships with manufacturers, allowing it to customize product sizes, packaging, and quantities to meet specific price points, an important capability in a business built around delivering compelling value. It also combines everyday essentials with seasonal, promotional, and discretionary merchandise, creating a treasure-hunt shopping experience that encourages repeat visits and impulse purchases.

Meanwhile, the company's extensive distribution infrastructure, automatic replenishment systems, and store-specific merchandise allocation capabilities help it manage inventory and serve thousands of relatively small-format stores efficiently. Dollar Tree has also spent decades building a brand around affordable merchandise, with its historical $1 price point being central to that identity. Even after moving to the $1.25 base price and introducing higher price tiers, Dollar Tree has a recognizable value proposition that is different from a conventional discount retailer simply offering periodic price reductions.

On November 4, CVS Health (CVS) reported its fiscal Q3 2026 results. The stock fell 12.5% that day, while the S&P 500 rose 1.6%. That same morning, management announced a plan to separate CVS into two independent publicly traded companies and gave a first look at 2027. So did the quarter itself let investors down?

How Did CVS Health's Quarter Compare With Forecasts?

The quarter came in well ahead of forecasts. CVS earned $2.09 a share on an adjusted basis, beating the $1.67 analysts expected. Revenue of $108 billion also topped the consensus estimate of $106 billion. Management also raised its full-year 2026 outlook for adjusted earnings per share to at least $8.20, from a range of $7.90 to $8.10.

Yet the stock moved in the opposite direction of similar companies. Elevance Health rose 4.9% on the day CVS fell, and UnitedHealth Group and Cigna gained as well. By the close on November 6, CVS was down 8.3% from its close before the report, while the S&P 500 had lost 2.5%. The fall came on a quarter that beat forecasts and lifted management's own outlook.

Are CVS Health's Earnings Still Recovering?

Against a year earlier, they are. Operating income for fiscal Q3 2026 came to $3.57 billion. That figure was up from $2.52 billion a year before, though it was lower than in the June quarter. Over the last twelve months, operating income reached $15.1 billion, compared with $10.7 billion for the twelve months before.

Management expects earnings to keep growing in 2027. The company now looks for at least $8.65 of adjusted earnings per share for 2027, up from the $8.45 floor it had talked about earlier. Management also expects another year of margin improvement at Aetna, its health insurance business. The exception is Health Services. For that segment, the company expects at least $7 billion of adjusted operating income in 2027, held back by a weaker selling season and the loss of members at health plan clients. Management called that year the low point for the segment's earnings.

The other change is the split. CVS Health will keep Aetna, Caremark and Oak Street, while CVS Pharmacy will hold the retail pharmacy stores, mail order and MinuteClinic. Management expects the separation to be tax free for U.S. federal income tax purposes and completed in the first half of 2028. Management also called the one-time and stranded costs of the split manageable.
